Group Architecture · Insurance first

Agent Harness Architecture on Azure

An agent is software we will run for years. We build it that way, once, for every company in the group.

IWhy

“Business goals the architecture needs to serve”The right architectureBusiness goals, the qualities they need, how we design, how we measure.

IIWhat

“The abstract architecture: the big picture”The harness systemVertical agents on shared horizontal assets. 18 concerns, 5 families, the statements we hold ourselves to.

IIIHow we build it

“How we bind: concern, port, binding, and four decisions first”Bound to AzureWhich Azure service fills each concern, what stays ours, and what it costs to leave. “Plain Python vs Pydantic AI vs LangGraph vs Claude Agent SDK”Inside the codeLoop options, ports and adapters, one turn end to end, patterns, contracts. “Policies and thresholds”Policy, state and contextWhere rules live, what the agent remembers, what the model sees. “Any server, any browser”Scale and resilienceMany servers, no sticky sessions, any browser; exactly-once effects, storm volume, several asks in one message.

IVTrust and safety

“What can go wrong: the risk register”What can go wrongA priority-ordered register: what can fail and how we handle it. “Defence in depth”SecurityDefence in depth, and the OWASP LLM Top 10 mapped to our controls. “Authentication and authorization”Authentication & authorizationThree auth questions, every identity, one payout end to end.

VProving it works

“Why evaluate, and the four places”EvaluationOffline, inline, online and continuous checks; rules, scores, dashboards. “The reusable rule library”Reusable assurance rules92 domain-agnostic rules, where they plug in, and the eval assets every agent reuses. “AgentTwin”AgentTwinA twin of the agent's world, not of the agent.

VICost

“Budgets and metering”Cost controlBudgets per turn, agent and team, and the LLM Cost Evaluation Framework. “Cost anti-patterns”Cost anti-patternsThe cost equation, explaining a change, 36 rules, and the architecture that prevents them.

VIIHow we work

“The spec family”The spec familySix specs, each answering one question, linked into one chain of proof. “Ways of working”Ways of workingOne COE, many agentic systems; the spec-driven SDLC with coding agents and human steering.

VIIIWorked example

“Sorting before the loop, and several asks in one message”The claims assistant, end to endWhich jobs need an agent, the sorting step, why the loop is a must, the daily bill, and how many agents an insurer needs.

Part 1 · Requirements · Section 1 · Functional requirements

Business goals the architecture needs to serve

What the business needs from the agent: the goals it must serve and the jobs it must do.

Architecture is a business decision that happens to be technical.

Create value

Drive ROIValue per case handled, not demos per quarter.lever → shared assets, cost per resolved case
Faster time to marketThe second agent ships in weeks, because it reuses the first one's road.lever → automated tests and evals, platform first, Lego blocks, plug-ins (slide How the architecture delivers faster time to market)
Customer trustA right answer, or an honest handoff to a person. Never a confident guess.lever → grounding, escalation

Run for years

Long-running productionAgents live for years. Models change every quarter. The system has to outlive both.lever → swappable parts, versioned config
Cost-optimal at scalePay for the answer, not the tokens.lever → routing, caching, budgets
Freedom to chooseNo model, cloud or vendor can hold us hostage.lever → ports and adapters, exit test

Stay safe, grow the group

Regulatory confidenceEvery decision can be shown to an auditor or to IRDAI, and replayed.lever → audit trail, replay, approvals
Reuse across the groupBuilt once for insurance, reused by the next group company.lever → horizontal assets
Business goal→needs a quality→designed in by principle→proved by a metric

Part 1 · Requirements · Section 2 · Non-functional requirements

Technical goals the architecture needs to meet

How well it must do the job: the technical goals, what each group of people expects, the qualities it must have, how we measure them, and what goes wrong without them.

The business goals only hold if the system underneath behaves. These are the behaviours we design for.

Right and safe

Grounded answersEvery amount, date and status comes from a system or a source, never from the model's memory.lever → grounding, reply rules
Safe actionsNothing irreversible happens without the right authority, and never twice.lever → permissions, approvals, idempotency
Hard to manipulateText from customers, documents and tools is data, never instructions.lever → fencing, guardrails, red team

Runs reliably

Survives failureA crash, retry or outage loses nothing and repeats nothing; the customer gets an honest reply.lever → checkpoints, typed failures, fallbacks
Scales outAny server takes any request; more users means more servers, not a redesign.lever → stateless servers, queues, leases
Visible and replayableEvery step of every turn can be seen, measured and re-run.lever → OpenTelemetry run record, replay

Changes safely

Swappable partsA model, cloud or tool changes without a rewrite.lever → ports and adapters, contracts
Proved before releaseNo change ships unless the golden set says it's no worse.lever → evaluation, release gates
Bounded costSpend is capped per turn, per agent and per team, and explained every day.lever → meter, budgets, gateway limits
Built once, reusedThe second agent reuses the first one's road.lever → horizontal assets, paved road
Technical goal→owned by a concern→bound to a service→proved by a test

Who it serves

Who the architecture serves

We have different roles, each with its own pain points and its own expectations from the system.

Business

pays for it and decides what is built

SDLC: “Business goals the architecture needs to serve” · Architecture: the motivation

Business ownerShow me it pays, and what each case costs.

Expects

  • ROI and cost per resolved claim
  • Share of cases handled end to end
  • A named owner for every agent
  • Run cost that is predictable month to month

Served bySeeChange

Program ownerTell me which agent to build next, and whether the programme is on track.

Expects

  • One view of every agent: stage, value, cost and risk
  • Shared assets reused, not rebuilt by each team
  • Use cases ranked by value and risk to pick what is next
  • Dependencies and approvals visible across teams

Served bySeeChange

Build

make the agent and test it

SDLC: “How we bind: concern, port, binding, and four decisions first” · Dev, “Plain Python vs Pydantic AI vs LangGraph vs Claude Agent SDK” · Testing

DevelopersLet me ship an agent without rebuilding the plumbing.

Expects

  • A paved-road template for a new agent
  • Models and tools behind stable interfaces
  • The whole agent runs locally, with recorded tool replies
  • Prompts versioned and reviewed with the code

Served byThinkAct

TestersProve it's right on every release, not just once.

Expects

  • Golden sets and scenarios run automatically in CI
  • Any failed conversation replays exactly
  • Mock tools and simulated customers
  • Scores compared release against release

Served byChangeSee

Deploy

get it live, safely and often

SDLC: “Policies and thresholds” · Deploy and release

Platform engineeringBuild it once, and let every team serve itself.

Expects

  • Shared assets with clear contracts
  • Everything as code: infrastructure, config, policy
  • Each agent has its own identity, and no secrets in code
  • Quotas and cost visible per team and per agent

Served byActControlChange

DeliveryGive me predictable releases and value I can show.

Expects

  • Lead time from idea to a live agent
  • Quality and cost dashboards per agent
  • Small staged rollouts, not big-bang launches
  • Risk sign-off built into the pipeline, with named owners

Served byChangeSee

Monitor

watch it live and fix it fast: observability

SDLC: “Any server, any browser” · Monitor

Operations & SRETell me before the customer does, and let me fix it fast.

Expects

  • One trace per conversation, end to end
  • Alerts on quality, cost and silence, not just uptime
  • A kill switch and one-step rollback

Served bySeeControl

Govern

make sure it stays safe and lawful

SDLC: every stage, from design to monitor

Risk & complianceShow me who decided, on what evidence, under which version.

Expects

  • Audit trail and replay of any decision

Served byControlSee

SecurityProve it can't be talked into doing harm.

Served byControlAct

SDLC: lives with the result

Served byThinkControl

Frontline staffClaims handlers and underwriters: hand me the case with the work done.

Expects

  • Full context when a case is handed over
  • Clear approval requests with the evidence
  • The agent drafts; I decide
  • I can override it and see why it suggested what it did

Served byControlThink

Part 1 · Requirements · Section 2 · Non-functional requirements

An agent is software

Everything we demand of software, we demand of agents, plus what a model makes harder.

The qualities the architecture must have, ISO/IEC 25010 plus four we add, are on What characteristics the architecture must have.

What a model makes harder

Same input, different outputTesting needs scored test sets, not single checks.
Reads untrusted text as instructionsA claim email can carry a hidden command.
Behaviour driftsA provider update can change answers overnight.
Cost varies per callOne long conversation can cost a hundred short ones.
Part 1 · Requirements · Section 2 · Non-functional requirements

The qualities: ISO/IEC 25010 plus four we add

What characteristics the architecture must have

The nine qualities of ISO/IEC 25010:2023, read for agents, plus four that agents make essential.

The nine qualities of ISO/IEC 25010:2023, read for agents

ISO 1Functional suitabilityDoes the right job, correctly and completely.Registers the claim with every required field.
ISO 2Performance efficiencyQuick, and frugal with tokens and compute.Answers a policy question in seconds.
ISO 3CompatibilityWorks with the systems we already run.Talks to policy admin and claims through their APIs.
ISO 4Interaction capabilityEasy to use, and explains itself.Cites the policy clause it relied on.
ISO 5ReliabilityKeeps working, and fails safely when it can't.Core system down: honest message and a reference.
ISO 6SecurityNo tricks get in, no data leaks out.A broker sees only their own clients.
ISO 7MaintainabilitySafe and cheap to change.A prompt change is reviewed and tested like code.
ISO 8FlexibilityAdapts to new models, clouds and lines of business.Motor today, health next quarter.
ISO 9SafetyCauses no harm, even when wrong. New in the 2023 edition.Never denies a claim on its own.
We addCostSpend is a design limit, measured per outcome.
We addObservabilityAny step of any conversation can be seen and replayed.
We addAuditabilityWho decided what, on which evidence, under which version.
We addResponsible AIFair, explainable, and open about being AI.

Every quality ties to a business goal, a principle and a metric in The golden thread; evaluation rules are grouped by these qualities too.

Part 1 · Requirements · Section 2 · Non-functional requirements

How we know it's working: what to measure

How we know it's working

We can't run what we can't see. Every incident has a clock.

Businessis it worth it?
Cost per resolved caseCases handled without a personCustomer satisfaction (CSAT)Time to settle a claimLead time for a new agent
Service healthis it running?
MTTD · MTTT · MTTR · MTBFAvailability against SLOError budget leftp95 latencySaturation and throttling
Delivery (DORA)can we change it safely?
Deployment frequencyLead time for changeChange failure rateFailed-deployment recovery time
Agent qualityis it right?
Task success rateGroundedness (answers backed by sources)Escalation rateHuman override rateTokens and cost per taskDrift against golden set
Part 1 · Requirements · Section 2 · Non-functional requirements

What goes wrong without them

On this page · 2 slides
  1. The gap between a demo and a system
  2. What goes wrong without the right architecture

The gap between a demo and a system

The demo shows the model. Production runs on everything underneath it.

What goes wrong without the right architecture

A demo hides these failures. Production finds every one of them, usually through a customer or a regulator.

What goes wrongWhat people seeWhat prevents it
Wrong customer's dataA customer reads someone else's claimIdentity carried to every tool; checks at the far end
Unauthorised or double actionsA payout without approval, or paid twiceApprovals the agent can't grant itself; idempotency keys
Hijacked by hidden textA claim document tells the agent to approve itselfUntrusted text fenced; guardrails at every position
Confident, wrong answersA wrong amount, date or status, stated as factGrounding; reply rules that block unsupported facts
Claims of action that never happened"Your claim is registered" when it wasn'tReply rules that check a real effect exists
Personal data leaksIdentity or bank details in a reply, log or traceRedaction before telemetry; PII checks on replies
Runaway costOne conversation loops and burns moneyBudgets per turn, agent and team; a meter on every call
Silent failureThe agent is politely wrong for weeks; nobody noticesOnline rules, sampled judges, alerts on quality, not just uptime
A release that hurts everyoneA prompt or model change degrades every answer at onceGolden-set gates, canary releases, one-step rollback
No audit trailA regulator asks who decided, and nobody can show itA run record per decision, versioned config, replay

The full register, with every risk's handling and status, is on Critical: must be in place before go-live.

Part 2 · Architecture · Section 3 · Challenges

Non-deterministic by nature

Why agentic systems are hard to architect: answers that vary from run to run, and an ecosystem with too many options that keeps moving.

Non-deterministic by nature

Ordinary software gives the same answer to the same question. An agent may not: a model decides, and a loop chooses its own path.

What it means for the architecture

Because the model may varyWeWhere it is covered
Not every step needs a modelDecide deterministic-first: rules and small classifiers where they are enough; the model only where it is a mustL4 Control loop
A loop can wander or never stopBound it: step, time and cost limits on every turnL4 Control loop · L13 Cost accounting
An answer can be wrong or unsafeCheck it: guards on the way in and out, typed contracts at every edge, a person for what it may not decideL7 Policy · L6 I/O contracts · L14 Human-in-the-loop
A past decision can't be re-run by asking againRecord it: every input, model reply and tool result, so it replays exactlyL9 Determinism & replay
One good run proves nothingMeasure it: golden sets and evaluators score many runs before and after releaseL12 Eval harness: eval design
Part 2 · Architecture · Section 3 · Challenges

The ecosystem became a universe

The ecosystem became a universe

In two years the agent ecosystem grew in every direction at once. For every concern an architect now has many products to choose from, and new ones every month.

How we cope with so many options

The challengeOur answerWhere it is covered
Too many products to compareChoose per concern, not per product: name the job first, then pick what fills itAgent Harness Engineering Concerns
Today's best pick is replaced next yearCode to an interface: every product sits behind a port; swapping it is a new adapter and a config changePorts and adapters · Tomorrow's changes
Choosing a model is guessworkDecide with evidence: the golden set scores each candidate on our own casesL2 Model invocation
Rebuilding what already existsReuse first, build the delta: the platform gives part, we code once what is common, each agent does only its own partPlatform, ours, each agent
Part 2 · Architecture · Section 3 · Challenges

Landing on a moving ship

Every provider is solving a different part of the puzzle, and the pieces keep moving. We aim for no-regret moves: decisions that keep us flexible as the ship turns.

Settled

Adopt the standard directly. No wrapper needed.

  • OpenTelemetry tracing and the GenAI conventions: the integration point for evaluation
  • Containers on managed compute
  • OAuth 2 and OpenID Connect for identity
  • PostgreSQL for state
  • Prometheus metrics and PromQL
  • Git, pull requests, CI
  • JSON Schema for tool contracts
Converging

Adopt the standard behind a thin port; track its versions.

  • MCP for tools (authorization still evolving)
  • A2A between agents
  • OpenAI-compatible and Messages API shapes
  • The AI gateway pattern
  • Prompt caching
  • Evaluation practice: golden sets, judges, pass^k
  • Guardrail detectors
Still moving

Choose for our scenarios, keep it behind a port, record the exit cost, set a review date.

  • Agent frameworks and loops
  • Hosted agent runtimes
  • Agent memory products
  • Agent identity (e.g. Entra Agent ID, preview)
  • Durable execution for agents
  • Hosted evaluation platforms
  • Which model is best for which job
settled · bind directlystill moving · bind behind a port, revisit

No-regret moves we make regardless

  • Own the loop and the context. That's our differentiator; it moves when we decide.
  • Ports and adapters everywhere. A moving concern can change product without touching the agent.
  • OpenTelemetry for every signal. Any evaluation or observability tool can read it.
  • Specs and evaluations independent of the stack. The same tests prove any binding.
  • Our data in our own store. Conversations, findings and approvals in PostgreSQL we control.
  • No hidden layers. We don't adopt anything whose behaviour our tests can't reach.
  • Every binding records its reason and exit cost, with a review date.
Moving concernOptions todayOur pick, for our scenariosRevisit whenDecided in
Control loopOwn Python loop · Pydantic AI · LangGraph · MS Agent Framework · hosted prompt agentsHand-written loop for customer-facing agents; Pydantic AI as the model layer everywhere, and its own loop allowed for simple A1–A3 agentsA framework offers trajectory checks we can test, or a .NET team joinsslide The loop is ours. What is it built from?
Long waits and approvalsDBOS · Temporal · Durable Task SchedulerDBOS on our PostgreSQLCompensation flows growslide Identity, guardrails, approvals, failure
ModelsGPT · Claude · bothBoth behind the gateway, chosen per job by the golden setEvery quarter, and on every major model releaseslide Model, context, loop, memory, knowledge
Agent identityApp registration + managed identity · Entra Agent IDApp registration + managed identityEntra Agent ID reaches general availabilityslide Every identity, mapped
Evaluation platformFoundry evaluation · our rules + AgentTwin · othersOur rules and AgentTwin; Foundry for generic judgesA platform runs our state oracles and rules as dataslide The horizontal eval assets
Long-term memoryNone · gated memory store · memory productsNone yetA use case needs memory across conversationsslide How we implement state
Our scenarios drive every pick: insurance first, then more group companies; Azure-first but able to move; several models; regulated, auditable, customer-facing. A choice that fits these today, sits behind a port and has a review date is a no-regret move, even if the ship turns.
Part 2 · Architecture · Section 4 · How to achieve them: guiding principles

Guiding principles (design philosophy)

The principles we follow to get those qualities, how much of software engineering we adopt, and the patterns that make the system easy to change.

Design philosophy

Simple by default. Agentic only where it has to be.

Systems thinking frames all of them. We optimise the whole claim journey, from the customer's first message to the payout, not one prompt or one model.
Design itso it stays understandable
  • Simple firstThe best agent step is the one we didn't need.
  • Deterministic firstIf a rule or a lookup can answer, the model is not called.
  • Separate concernsEach concern has one home, so it can change alone.
  • Readable, self-explanatoryCode, names and traces explain themselves; a newcomer follows one turn without a guide.
  • Fail fast, at every role and functionSurface a problem at the earliest point: a bad spec in review, a failing test before merge, an unpriced model or wrong rule version at startup, bad tool arguments before the call.
  • Lego blocks, joined by contractsEach block can be swapped or tested alone; a change touches only what depends on its contract.
  • Contracts at every edgeTyped inputs and outputs. No guessing between parts.
Scale itso the tenth agent is cheap
  • Platform thinkingBuild the road once. Every agent drives on it.
  • ReuseShared assets, not copies of them.
  • Self-serveA team ships an agent without filing a ticket.
  • Automation firstIf people do it twice, a pipeline does it next time: tests, gates, deploys, alert packs, dashboards.
  • Best practices built inTemplates, gates and shared assets enforce the practice. A document only describes it.
  • Built for a fast SDLCEvery design choice should make specifying, building, testing and releasing faster. The golden path takes a new agent live in weeks.
  • EvolvableSwap a model like a part, not like a heart transplant.
Control itso we can trust it
  • TransparentEvery answer shows its working and its sources.
  • Human in controlAgents propose. People decide on money and cover.
  • Secure by designEach agent has its own identity and the least access it needs.
  • Limit the blast radiusSmall canary releases, per-agent budgets, kill switches, least privilege: one failure stays small.
  • MeasuredIf it isn't measured, it isn't in production.
Part 2 · Architecture · Section 4 · How to achieve them: guiding principles

How the architecture delivers faster time to market

Speed does not come from cutting corners. It comes from not redoing work: machines check every change, the platform does what it already does, and a new feature is added without editing what works.

LeverWhat we doWhy it is fasterApplied in
Automated testingUnit, contract and integration tests, with recorded tool replies, run on every change in CINo manual regression round; a change is checked in minutes, not daysslides Test the software, evaluate the agent, From laptop to release: the gates
Automated evalsGolden sets, AgentTwin scenarios and evaluators score every release against a barA scorecard replaces a review meeting; a model or prompt change ships the day it passesslides Scores and gates, One YAML: where each evaluator runs
Adopt what the platform offersGateway, content safety, tracing, hosting and identity come from Azure; we code only what no product coversWe build the delta, not the plumbing; the second agent starts on a ready roadslides Platform, ours, the agent's: the split per concern, What we code once, and what stays with each team
Lego blocks, small blast radiusEach block has one job and a contract; blocks join only through contractsA change touches one block and its tests, so less to review, less to retest, less to breakslides Lego blocks, joined by contracts, A change knows what to test
Inversion of control, open/closedThe harness depends on ports; products and checks plug in through adapters named in YAMLNew things are added, never edited in: open for extension, closed for modificationslides Ports in code: the class diagram, Evaluators as plug-ins: configure, don't code

Example: adding a new evaluator, open/closed

# 1 · one new class, behind the evaluator port
class PayoutWording(Evaluator):
    """Never promise cover in a reply."""
    def check(self, req: EvalRequest) -> EvalResult:
        ...
# 2 · two new lines in evaluators.yaml
evaluators:
  payout_wording: {kind: rule}     # new

positions:
  reply:                            # inline: blocks
    - {use: no_ungrounded_entity, on_fail: safe_reply}
    - {use: payout_wording, on_fail: safe_reply}   # new

Nothing in the harness, the loop or the other evaluators changes, so their tests still hold and only the new check needs its own. Swapping a model, a vector store or a channel works the same way: a new adapter and a config line.

Adopt software engineering to the maximum: design, build, test

Decades of engineering practice already solve most of our problems. We adopt as much of it as we can, and adapt only where a model makes it different.

The same release discipline as any critical system, plus checks for what a model can get wrong.

AreaPracticeWhat it means for our agentsApplied in

Infrastructure as codeBicep or Terraform for every environmentslide Release, config, evaluation

What's genuinely new for agents sits on top of these practices, not instead of them: scored evaluation of the model's choices, a fence around untrusted text, versioning prompt + model + policy together, and judging outcomes from the world's state rather than from the words.

The Twelve-Factor App, applied to agents

The cloud-native baseline every service already meets. Our agents meet all twelve; the agent-specific rules sit on top.

#FactorThe ruleFor our agentsApplied in
1CodebaseOne codebase in version control, deployed many timesOne repo per agent; dev, test and prod are deploys of the same codeslide The spec-driven SDLC, with humans steering
2DependenciesDeclare and pin every dependencyPinned packages, and pinned model versions tooslide From counter to alert
3ConfigConfig in the environment, not in codeAGENT_* settings from App Configuration; budgets and endpoints per environmentslide Threshold example: the cost ceiling per turn
4Backing servicesDatabases and queues are attached, swappable resourcesPostgreSQL, the model gateway and MCP servers sit behind portsslide Ports in code: the class diagram
5Build, release, runStrictly separate stagesImmutable image; release = image + config; what runs is what was assessedslide Release, config, evaluation
6ProcessesStateless processes; state in backing servicesStateless containers, stateful agentslide Stateless or stateful?
7Port bindingThe service exposes itself on a portThe agent serves HTTP; Container Apps routes to itslide One turn, end to end
8ConcurrencyScale out by running more processesMore Container Apps replicas; nothing held in memoryslide How we implement state
9DisposabilityFast start, graceful shutdownCheckpoint every turn; a killed container loses nothingslide How we implement state
10Dev/prod parityKeep environments alikeEnvironments differ only by configurationslide Same code, different adapters
11LogsLogs as event streamsOpenTelemetry spans and counters to App Insights and Prometheusslide Two signals, two stores
12Admin processesOne-off tasks as separate processesWatch job, canary and cost engine as Container Apps Jobsslide Where the rules plug in

The Twelve-Factor App was written by engineers at Heroku around 2011 as a method for building services that deploy, scale and run cleanly in the cloud. What it doesn't cover, we add: versioning prompt + model + policy together (factor 5), and judging behaviour by evaluation, not only by logs (factor 11).

Design patterns

Design patterns we use

Nothing exotic. Proven software patterns, applied to the parts a model makes risky.

KindPatternWhat it isBenefitExample in our agent
StructurePorts and adaptersThe agent depends on interfaces (Protocols); products plug in as adaptersSwap Azure, a test fake or another cloud without touching agent codeLLMClient → PydanticAIClient on Azure, ScriptedClient in tests
StructureComposition root (dependency injection)All wiring happens in one function at startup; objects receive what they needOne place names Azure; everything else is testableentrypoint.build() called from run_server.main()
StructureDecoratorWrap an object to add behaviour while keeping its interfaceRetries and recording without changing the clientResilientLLM(Recorder(PydanticAIClient(…)))
StructureGateway (single choke point)Every model call goes through one doorLimits, metrics, routing and swaps in one placeAPIM AI gateway + the LLMClient port
StructureAnti-corruption layerA facade that speaks the model's language over legacy APIsThe model sees intents, not 60 endpointsDedicated MCP tool register_claim over the claims REST API
StructureMethod objectA long algorithm becomes an object that holds its stateThe loop stays readable and testable step by step_Run holds messages, keys and the screen for loop.run
Control flowDeterministic first (router)Rules answer what rules can before any model callCheaper, faster, predictablerouter.route → Refuse / Escalate / Direct / Agentic
Control flowChain of checks, fail closedOrdered checks at declared positions; the first block wins; errors blockBad replies and actions stopped by defaultScreen.at(PRE_MODEL … REPLY) → policy.enforce
Control flowStrategyRules are swappable functions passed in as dataAdd or version a rule without touching the loopOUTPUT_RULES list: no_ungrounded_entity, no_pii_echo
Control flowDiscriminated result typesEvery outcome is a named type the caller must handleNo silent failures; HTTP status follows the typeTurnResult = Completed | NeedsApproval | Refused | Escalated | Failed
ResilienceRetry with backoff + circuit breakerBounded, visible retries; stop calling a failing providerOutages degrade gracefully instead of cascadingResilientLLM(attempts, backoff, breaker, throttle)
ResilienceBulkhead (bounded concurrency)Cap fan-out per step and per turnOne turn can't fire fifty writesmax_tool_calls_per_step = 8, gather_bounded
ResilienceBudget / kill switchCeilings outside the model's control stop work in flightRunaway loops and costs are containedBudgets: 12 steps, $0.50, 60 s; Meter.exceeded
CorrectnessIdempotency keyEach side effect carries a key; repeats return the first resultA retry never pays a claim twiceIdempotencyKey(run_id, step, iteration) + Requests.claim
CorrectnessDurable workflow (long waits)Waits that last days live in a workflow engine, not in memoryApprovals survive restarts and deploysPayout approval as a DBOS / Temporal workflow
CorrectnessSaga / compensationEach action declares how to undo itPartial failures can be unwoundReverse a payout if the approval is later withdrawn
CorrectnessCheckpoint (memento)State is saved whole after every turnA conversation resumes after a crashCheckpointStore.checkpoint(run_id, state)
CorrectnessImmutable config snapshotPrompt, model and policy resolved once, fingerprinted, recordedEvery result traces to the exact versionRunConfig + agent.config.fingerprint on every span
TestabilityTest doubles and simulatorFakes and a simulated world stand in for real systemsFast, free, deterministic testsScriptedClient, FaultyProvider, AgentTwin projection
TestabilityRecord and replay (cassette)Real responses recorded once, replayed in testsReal behaviour without network or costRecorder / Player around the LLMClient
OperationsObserver (span processor)Counters are derived from finished spansMetrics without metric code in the loopRunNumbers(SpanProcessor) counts terminations and spend
OperationsOut-of-band evaluatorA job beside the agent judges finished turnsEvaluation can never slow or change a replyWatch job: online rules W-01 … W-21
OperationsSynthetic transaction (canary)A fake customer exercises the real path on a scheduleBreaks found with no real trafficCanary every 10 min as a synthetic identity
OperationsCanary release + feature flagsNew versions get a small share of traffic firstBad releases reach few customersContainer Apps revisions + App Configuration
SecurityToken exchange (on-behalf-of)The agent acts with the user's identity, never a master keyAn agent can't exceed the user's own accessEntra on-behalf-of to the policy admin system

Class names come from the reference agent; examples are recast for insurance. DBOS, Entra on-behalf-of and the APIM gateway are the planned Azure bindings.

Part 2 · Architecture · Section 4 · How to achieve them: guiding principles

Ports and adapters (inversion of control)

On this page · 2 slides
  1. Ports in code: the class diagram
  2. Same code, different adapters

Ports in code: the class diagram

The Agent asks for interfaces, never for products. The composition root decides what plugs in.

Same code, different adapters

Moving to Azure means a handful of new adapters and one new composition root. The agent's code doesn't change.

The composition root on Azure (illustrative)

# the only file that knows we run on Azure
settings = Settings()                     # AGENT_* env vars
llm = ResilientLLM(PydanticAIClient(      # our port, Pydantic AI inside
        OpenAIChatModel(settings.model,  # via the APIM AI gateway
          provider=AzureProvider(openai_client=azure_client(
            settings.apim_url, token=managed_identity)))))
if settings.record:
    llm = Recorder(llm)                   # cassettes
pool = postgres_pool(settings.pg_url)     # Azure PostgreSQL
tools = MCPToolClient(
    MCPTransport(mcp_client(settings.mcp_url),
                 exchange=EntraOnBehalfOf(settings)),
    requests=PostgresRequests(pool))
agent = entrypoint.build(
    llm=llm, tools=tools,
    store=PostgresCheckpointStore(pool),
    deliveries=PostgresRequests(pool),
    approvals=DbosApprovals(pool),
    escalations=DbosEscalations(pool),
    config=resolve(settings), clock=time.time)
app = serve.build(agent, issuer=Issuer(
        RemoteJWKS.discover(settings.entra_issuer)))
tel.configure(exporter=azure_monitor)     # spans + metrics
PortReference agentAzureChange
LLMClientGroqClient (OpenAI SDK)PydanticAIClient: Pydantic AI's model layer behind our port; Azure OpenAI and Claude through APIM1 new adapter
ToolClientGatedTools + MCPTransportUnchanged; MCP servers on Container Appsconfig
CheckpointStorePostgresCheckpointStoreUnchanged, on Azure PostgreSQLconfig
RequestsPostgresRequestsUnchanged, on Azure PostgreSQLconfig
Approvals · EscalationsTemporal adaptersDBOS adapters (or keep Temporal)2 new adapters
Exchange · KeySourceKeycloak exchange, RemoteJWKSEntra on-behalf-of; RemoteJWKS pointed at Entra1 new adapter
TelemetryOTLP → collectorAzure Monitor OTel exporterconfig
ChannelChatwoot APIChatwoot on Container Apps; Communication Services for WhatsApp1 new adapter
Clock · SessionStoretime.time · PostgresUnchangednone

Today the reference agent wires adapters in code from settings. The harness profile (ABS) records the choice for review, but isn't read at runtime. The adapter names on Azure (PydanticAIClient, EntraOnBehalfOf, DbosApprovals) are proposed names, not existing code; the Pydantic AI calls are illustrative and must be checked against the pinned version.

A change knows what to test

No big-bang regression, no breakage after a fix. Every change finds its own blast radius before it's merged.

Kind of changeWhat runsWhy that's enough
An adapter (e.g. the PostgreSQL store)That port's behaviour suite + its integration testBlocks above see only the Protocol, which didn't change

Part 2 · Architecture · Section 5 · The abstract architecture

A word of caution: this is a north star, a corpus that might not apply to every agent

On this page · 2 slides
  1. A word of caution: this is a north star, a corpus that might not apply to every agent
  2. Ten shapes of agent

This document describes the whole corpus. Most agents need a slice of it. When a knife is enough, don't forge a sword.

The downside

A simple agent can become complex

Followed blindly, the north star adds responsibilities, code and infrastructure an agent doesn't need. Delivery slows, there is more to maintain and more to break, and teams copy everything "to be safe".

The upside

We know the whole corpus

Because everything is mapped, we choose deliberately for each agent and use case. Nothing important is forgotten, and anything left out is a known, owned decision rather than an accident.

Precautions, so the north star doesn't make agents heavy

1

Start from the archetype

Begin with what this kind of agent owes, never with the whole catalog (the ten shapes: slide Ten shapes of agent).

2

Scale by risk

A read-only FAQ agent and a payout agent get different controls.

3

Deterministic first

If rules can do the job, there is no model, and no agent.

4

Reuse, don't rebuild

Complexity lives once in the platform's shared assets, not in every agent.

5

Name the delta

Every component must answer a concern this agent owes, or it isn't built.

6

Leave out on purpose

A skipped item is an accepted gap with an owner and a review date, not silence.

7

Add on evidence

An incident, a finding or a new obligation brings a capability in, not a hunch.

8

Review for excess too

Architecture review asks "what can we remove?" as often as "what's missing?"

Every concern in this document must earn its place in a given agent. The north star tells us what exists; the agent's spec decides what it needs.

Ten shapes of agent

The shape of an agent, not its domain, decides what it owes. Two questions draw every line: who controls the flow, and what does the output touch?

IDArchetypeWhat it isWho controls the flowWhat the output touchesBiggest new riskInsurance example
A1Single-Turn TransformOne call in, one answer out. No tools, retrieval or memoryOur codeA person reads itPlain wrong contentSummarise a claim note for a handler
A2Structured ExtractorOutput is a typed object that code consumesOur codeDownstream codeQuality failures become type failuresRead a claim form or repair estimate into fields
A3Grounded AnswererRetrieves from a corpus, then writes an answerOur codeA person, citing sourcesRetriever and writer fail separatelyAnswer from policy wordings and SOPs
A4Conversational AssistantMulti-turn and stateful, but takes no actionOur code, across turnsA person, over a conversationState and memory across turnsBroker desk Q&A
A5Deterministic WorkflowA fixed graph with model calls at the nodesOur code (the graph)Systems, step by stepThe seams between stepsRenewal reminder pipeline
A6Tool-Using AgentThe model chooses tools, order, and when to stopThe modelReal systems, through toolsControl flow moves into the model: the biggest jumpClaims FNOL intake · policy servicing
A7Multi-Agent SystemAgents delegate to each otherSeveral modelsSystems, via handoffsBoundaries, budgets, containmentFNOL hands a suspicious claim to fraud signals
A8Artifact ProducerOutput is code, SQL, config or a document that gets usedThe modelAn executed or shipped artifactThe artifact runs, so verify by running itSQL for an actuarial report · a drafted endorsement
A9Autonomous OperatorRuns on a trigger or schedule, unattendedThe model, nobody watchingReal systems, unattendedSide effects with no one in the loopNightly chase of missing claim documents
A10Classifier · Router · JudgeIts output steers other machineryThe model's verdictOther componentsErrors are invisible unless checked themselvesClaims triage router · fraud flag · an LLM judge
Tags, not a tree. An agent carries every shape that applies. Claims FNOL is A6 and A4; with a handoff to fraud signals it is also A7. It owes the union of what each shape owes.
Why it matters: the archetype is where slicing the north star starts. Of 118 harness capabilities, a deterministic workflow (A5) owes 61 and a tool-using agent (A6) owes 76.

Definitions come from the AI Assurance Catalog's taxonomy, shared by both catalogs. Mapping our agents to archetypes is on slide Archetypes decide what's owed.

Part 2 · Architecture · Section 6 · The Azure architecture

How we bind: concern, port, binding, and four decisions first

How we bind the design to Azure, the whole system on one page, family by family, every service we use, what stays ours, and how a new agent comes aboard.

On this page · 2 slides

Concern, port, binding

The specs fix the concern and the port. Azure only fills the binding.

Four decisions first

Decide who owns the loop. Everything else follows from that.

AWho owns the control loop?
✓Our hand-written loop on Container AppsPydantic AI as the model layer underneath. Step budget, no-progress check and cost ceiling stay visible. Nothing is lost.
◐Microsoft Agent FrameworkOnly if the team is .NET-first. Trajectory checks must be proved again.
✗Foundry Agent Service prompt agentLoop, retries and replay are hidden, so we can't assure them.
BHow do we reach models?
✓APIM AI gatewayOne door, one identity, one bill. Token limits and token metrics at the gateway.
✗Each agent calls the SDKNo single place for limits, metrics or swaps.
CWho hosts the models?
✓Microsoft Foundry ModelsGPT and Claude deployments in one catalogue. Which model is a choice we make per job (Model, context, loop, memory, knowledge).
DWhere does our code run?
✓Azure Container AppsAgents, MCP servers and the chat desk. Revisions give canary releases.
◐AKSWhen we need GPUs, mesh or very large scale.

Which models do agents use?Open decision · our recommendation
1GPT on Azure OpenAIStrong and Azure-native. Highest exit cost: GPT-5-class models aren't on other clouds.
2Claude in FoundryThe same Messages API on Azure, AWS and Google Cloud, so it's portable.
3Both, behind the gatewayRoute per job. The golden set picks the model, not preference.
4Azure model routerAzure picks a model per prompt. A candidate per job when difficulty varies, not the default (Model router: where it fits).

Recommend option 3. Claude in Foundry is the default for long-lived workloads because it moves across clouds. GPT, or model router, is used wherever it scores better on our golden set for that job. With no golden set yet, start on the default and let the seed set decide (Day one: no golden set yet).

Identity, guardrails, approvals, failure

80% of this is ordinary Azure security. The other 20% is agent-specific, and that's where the risk is.

ConcernAzure bindingStays oursOther options
L16 IdentityEntra ID for staff · managed identity for every agent · on-behalf-of exchange to systems of recordCustomer and broker ID taken from the verified token, checked where the action runsPolicyholder login: see below

Which engine runs approvals and long waits?Open decision · our recommendation
1Durable Task SchedulerAzure-native and managed. Its own programming model; workflows in flight can't move clouds.
2Temporal (Cloud or AKS)Portable and strongest for undo flows. One more platform to buy or run.
3DBOS on our PostgreSQLPortable, a library, no new infrastructure. Best for simple waits.

Recommend option 3 to start. Move to Temporal when compensation flows grow. Choose Durable Task Scheduler only if the group commits to Azure for good. Full comparison: slide Durable waits: DBOS, Temporal or Durable Task Scheduler?.

How do policyholders sign in?Open decision · our recommendation
1Entra External IDAzure-native, supports on-behalf-of. Password hashes can't be exported.
2Federate the existing portal loginNo second login for customers. Uses standard OIDC.
3Cloud-neutral identity providerPortable. One more product to run.

Recommend option 2 if a policyholder login already exists. If not, use option 1 with standard claims only, and keep the customer ID in our own database.

Platform, ours, the agent's: the split per concern

A horizontal asset is what we code once on top of the platform. Not what Azure gives us, and not what each agent still writes.

Example · evaluation

25 · 45 · 30

  • Platform (25%): Foundry evaluators as judges, the AI Red Teaming Agent, evaluation runs to view and compare.
  • Ours, once (45%): the golden case format, AgentTwin, graders, the 92 assurance rules, the case factory, the model-selection run, the eval report, the release gates.
  • Each agent (30%): its own cases, its own world in AgentTwin, its own thresholds.
The rule

z shrinks over time

When two agent teams write the same code, it moves from z into y and gets an owner. When the platform starts offering what we built, y moves into x and we delete ours. Each asset is reviewed against both directions once a quarter.

What stays ours

Azure gives us the plumbing. The parts that make an agent trustworthy stay in our code.

The control loopLimits we can see across the whole conversation.
Context assemblyWhat the model sees, and why.
Policy positionsWhere each check runs, in which order.
Tool designOne tool per business intent.
Replay recorderNo Azure service does this.
Span contractWhat every step must record.
Undo and idempotencySafe retries on payouts and changes.
Cost per outcomeCost per claim, not per call.

This is also why the Foundry prompt-agent route was dropped on Four decisions first: it moves these parts out of sight, and then no test can reach them.

Part 2 · Architecture · Section 6 · The Azure architecture

Onboarding a new agent

A new insurance agent is eight steps on the platform, not a new project.

  1. Write what it must doIts job, its limits, and what must always be true.FNOL: register a motor claim; never promise a payout
  2. Pick its archetypeThe archetype says which capabilities and ports it owes.conversational agent with actions
  3. Confirm who owns the loopDefault: ours. Change it only with a reason.ours on Container Apps
  4. Bind each portIn order: same engine managed, then Azure service, then open source on Azure, then our own code.model → gateway; state → PostgreSQL
  5. List the gapsEvery uncovered concern is a build item or an accepted risk.gap list signed by the owner
  6. Run the same testsScenarios, golden set and red-team, unchanged.300 past claims + attack cases
  7. Run the exit testEvery service has an answer for "what if it disappears?"exit note per service
  8. Release small, watch closelyCanary revision, named owner, registry entry, dashboards on day one.5% of FNOL traffic first

A stress test of the design. The loop column is almost empty, and that's the point.

changes · re-verified only · empty: untouched. Most changes land in spec, config, one adapter, and the evaluations that prove them. A design whose loop changed every time would be shaky; here the loop is touched only, and lightly, by a new agent-to-agent handoff. This is the design's claim: some rows are already proven in the reference agent (model and store swaps behind their ports); the rest become drills, such as swapping the model in a canary each quarter, so the claim stays true.

Models, frameworks and services will change. Each one should be a config edit or one adapter, proved by the same tests.

Code lock-in is cheap. Lock-in to data, workflows and models is expensive.

The agent harness: one block

The big picture, then one message from end to end, then the concerns placed along that journey, in the order it meets them.

The agent harness: one block between the user and the model

A customer never talks to the model directly. Everything in between is the agent harness, and the concerns are what's inside it.

End to End Journey Flow

78 steps between pressing send and reading the reply. Three journeys: getting the message to the right route, the agent's loop, and the reply with everything that happens after it.

4Status cardAPIIf a claim is open, the window shows its current status before the customer asks.Proposed
5Live connectionBrowser ↔ Web PubSub or ChatwootThe window opens a live connection, so a reply can arrive from any server.Proposed
The customer acts
6Types or tapsBrowserThe customer types a message, or taps a button such as "Check my claim".
7Message IDBrowserThe window gives the message a unique ID and keeps it if it has to resend.Built
8SendBrowser → Front DoorThe window sends the message, the sign-in token and the ID.Built
9WaitingBrowserThe window shows the message as sent and a "thinking" indicator.Proposed
Arriving at our server
10Front DoorAzure Front DoorFront Door filters attacks and passes the request to any healthy server. No sticky sessions.Azure
11ReceivedAPI server (Python)Our Python server receives the message.Built
12Check identityAPI serverIt checks the sign-in token and works out who the customer is and what they may do.Built
13Load conversationAPI → PostgreSQLIt loads the customer's latest conversation.Built
14Duplicate checkAPI → PostgreSQLIt looks up the message ID. A repeat gets the earlier answer instead of a second run.Built
15Shared recordAPI → ChatwootIt adds the message to the customer's conversation in the desk, so staff can see it.Built (Chatwoot adapter)
Sorting the message
16Rules firstAPI serverButtons, the conversation's state (a form in progress) and simple patterns decide the route when they can.Proposed
17Local classifierAPI serverOtherwise a small classifier inside our server labels the message, with a confidence score.Proposed
18Small modelAPI → gateway → FoundryIf the classifier isn't sure, a small model picks the label.Proposed
19Several asksAPI serverA message with several asks is split into parts, each routed on its own.Proposed
20Route chosenAPI serverThe message goes to a fixed flow, policy search, the agent, a person, or a polite refusal.Built (routes)
Fixed flow (no agent)
21Look upAPI → MCP → claims systemThe flow fetches the facts it needs from the claims system.Built
22Fill the templateAPI serverIt fills an approved reply template. No model writes the answer.Built
23Go to the reply checksAPI serverThe reply joins the same checks as every other reply (stage after the loop).Built

Part 3 · Design · Section 8 · High level design

Journey 2 of 3: the queue and the loop

The whole journey in plain English (2 of 3): the queue and the loop

The loop is a short list of steps, repeated. Every step has a check before it and a saved point after it.

#StepRuns inWhat happens, in plain EnglishStatus
Queueing the work
24Into the queueAPI → Service BusAgent and search turns go into a queue with a priority and a deadline.To build
25Picked upWorkerAny free worker takes the turn and holds a lease, so no other worker runs it.To build
26One at a timeWorker → PostgreSQLOnly one turn per conversation runs at once; a second message waits its turn.To build
27Too late?WorkerA turn past its deadline isn't started; the customer is told when to expect a reply.To build
Before the loop
28Start the runWorkerThe agent starts a run with limits on steps, time and cost.Built
29Allowed toolsWorker → MCPIt lists only the tools this customer may use.Built
30Build what the model seesWorkerIt puts together the instructions, tools, history and new message, always in the same order.Built
31Mark untrusted textWorkerAnything that came from outside, such as document text, is marked as data, not instructions.Built
32Keep it short enoughWorkerIf the history is too long, older exchanges in the middle are trimmed.Built
Inside the loop: the model
33Our input checkWorkerOur rules check what's about to go to the model, such as an injection attempt.Built
34Into the gatewayWorker → APIMThe request goes to our AI gateway, never straight to a model.Built (adapter)
35Gateway: sign inAPIMThe gateway signs in to Foundry with its managed identity; the agent holds no model key.Azure
36Gateway: allowed modelsAPIMIt checks this agent may use the model it asked for.Azure
37Gateway: token limitAPIMIt checks the agent's and customer tier's tokens per minute; over the limit gets a polite 429.Azure
38Gateway: edge screenAPIM → Content SafetyOptionally, it screens the request with Content Safety at the edge.Azure (optional)
39Gateway: pick a backendAPIMIt sends the call to the first healthy backend: provisioned first, then pay-as-you-go, then a second region.Azure
40Azure input checkFoundry guardrailAzure screens the input for harm and jailbreaks.Azure
41The model answersFoundry modelThe model reads the request and writes its response.Azure
42Azure output checkFoundry guardrailAzure screens what the model wrote.Azure
43Gateway: count tokensAPIM → Azure MonitorOn the way back, the gateway records tokens by agent, model and tier.Azure
44Gateway: not usedAPIMSemantic cache and full prompt logging stay off: answers are personal, and our own redacted record is the log.
45Count the costWorkerThe call's cost is added to the run's spend. Past the ceiling, the run stops.Built
46Answer or tool?WorkerThe model either gives an answer or asks for a tool.Built
Inside the loop: a tool
47Is it allowed?WorkerBefore a tool runs, our rules check it's permitted and that the customer asked for it.Built
48Needs a person?Worker → DBOSIf the action needs approval, such as a payout, the run pauses and asks an adjuster.To build
49Gateway for toolsAPIM → MCP serverThe gateway checks the token and rate limit before the MCP server sees the call.Azure
50Call the toolWorker → MCP → claims systemThe tool is called with a key that stops a retry from acting twice.Built
51Check the resultWorkerThe result is size-capped, checked for hidden instructions, and marked as data.Built
52Azure tool checkFoundry agent guardrailFor Foundry agents, Azure can also screen tool calls and results.Azure (preview)
53Save progressWorker → PostgreSQLProgress is saved, so a crash resumes from here, not from the start.Built
Inside the loop: when to stop
54LimitsWorkerIf steps, time or cost run out, the loop stops.Built
55No progressWorkerIf the model keeps repeating itself, the loop stops.Built
56RepeatWorkerOtherwise the loop goes back to the model with the new information.Built

Rows marked Azure are Foundry guardrails we can switch on; our own checks run whether or not they are on.

Part 3 · Design · Section 8 · High level design

Journey 3 of 3: the reply, people, and what happens afterwards

The whole journey in plain English (3 of 3): the reply, people, and what happens afterwards

The customer sees one reply. Behind it: rules on the way out, a person when needed, and checks that keep running after the turn.

#StepRuns inWhat happens, in plain EnglishStatus
After the loop: the reply
57Our reply rulesWorkerOur rules check the draft reply: no made-up claim numbers, dates, offers or personal data.Built
58Promise checkWorkerAny promise, such as "we'll call you", must be backed by a real task, or the turn escalates.Built
59Safe fallbackWorkerIf a rule blocks, the reply becomes a safe message or a hand-off to a person.Built
60Save togetherWorker → PostgreSQLThe conversation and the reply are saved in one step, so neither exists without the other.Built (state) · outbox to build
61DeliverSender → Web PubSub or ChatwootThe reply is sent to whichever window or channel is open.Proposed
62ShownBrowserThe customer sees the reply. A refreshed or new window loads it too.Proposed
When a person is needed
63Hand-off ticketWorker → ChatwootThe question, what the agent found, and what's missing go to the human desk.To build
64Bot steps backChatwootThe conversation moves to a person, who sees the full history.To build
65WaitsDBOS on PostgreSQLApprovals and hand-offs wait as saved records with timers; any server resumes them.To build
66Decision returnsAPI → DBOSThe adjuster's decision or the desk's resolution resumes the waiting work exactly once.To build
After the turn (out of sight)
67TraceWorker → Application InsightsEvery step is recorded, with personal data removed.Built
68CountersWorker → Managed PrometheusCounters update: turns, refusals, steps, cost.Built
69Online rulesScheduled jobA job reads finished turns, runs the same rules again, and stores findings.Built on Langfuse · Azure to build
70Sampled judgesFoundry continuous evaluationA sample of turns is scored by evaluators such as groundedness and task adherence.To adopt
71AlertsManaged PrometheusRules watch windows of turns and alert on spikes, such as refusals or cost.Built
72Daily costScheduled jobThe cost engine explains yesterday's spend and suggests fixes.v0
73CanaryScheduled jobSynthetic customers run real cases on a schedule, to catch breakage early.Built
74DashboardsManaged GrafanaPeople see health, quality, safety and cost for each agent.Built (template)
Before the next release
75Golden casesCIThe new version answers the golden cases inside a simulated world (AgentTwin).Built
76Red teamCIAttacks are run against it; their success rate must stay low.Partial
77ReportCIThe eval report compares results with the last release and explains any change.To build
78GateCIIf anything got worse, the release is blocked.Built

Built = exists in the reference agent today. To build / Proposed = in this design, not yet coded. Azure = a platform feature we switch on.

Part 1 · RunServer The server starts

Before anyone types, the container starts and builds everything once: it reads which adapters to use, fetches secrets from Key Vault, connects to PostgreSQL and the claims system, starts DBOS, and opens the web routes. Container Apps scales the agent to zero when idle, so every cold start (about 30 seconds) runs this whole part.

The journey steps it covers

StepWhat happens (from the 78)On Azure todayHow
—Not one of the 78 steps: they start when a person acts. This is the set-up they all rely on.runs today

The code, in the order it runs

  1. agent.Dockerfile: CMD python -m claims_fnol_app --port 8000, with CLAIMS_FNOL_ENV=azure
  2. F claims_fnol_app/__main__.py:21 main(): async with compose(adapters.plan(overlay())) as app, then uvicorn
  3. F claims_fnol_app/compose.py:60 overlay(): picks config/azure.yaml from CLAIMS_FNOL_ENV
  4. H adapters/__init__.py:197 plan(): reads the overlay and the profile it extends (harness-profile.yaml → stacks/azure.yaml); looks up each adapter in ADAPTERS; a secret must be a {key_vault: …} reference, never a literal
  5. F compose.py:107 compose() → H adapters.compose: builds the ports in order: secrets → config → telemetry → model → state → records → identity → tool_runtime → approval
  6. H adapters/state.py:68: refuses a database URL without sslmode=require; runs migrations/*.sql (the agent_state tables)
  7. H adapters/waits.py:66: DBOS(config=…), DBOS.launch(): the durable waits for approvals and escalations
  8. F claims_fnol/entrypoint/__init__.py:378 build(): makes the Agent, wrapped as Logged(Switched(Agent)) (log line, then kill switch)
  9. F claims_fnol_app/edge.py:84 edge.build(): mounts /, POST /chat, /ops/desk (from H serve.build), GET /opening, and /signin, /signin/callback, /signin/refresh, /signin/logout
  10. S claims-system.Dockerfile → S __main__.py:150: the second container: migrate, seed --if-empty, serve on 9050 at /mcp; S server.py:266 registers 8 tools

Part 2 · SignIn Sign-in with Entra

The policyholder opens the sign-in link and is sent to Microsoft. Microsoft sends them back with a one-time code; our server swaps it for tokens, checks them, and decides where they land: the chat for a policyholder, the desk for a handler. This is where the first live run found its bugs (F-114, F-115).

The journey steps it covers

StepWhat happens (from the 78)On Azure todayHow
2Who they are: the window knows the customer from the sign-in.different todayour own /signin page with Entra, not a portal's sign-in

The code, in the order it runs

  1. F claims_fnol_app/signin_flow.py:116 start(): makes a Flow (state, PKCE verifier, nonce), seals it in the signin_flow cookie, redirects 303 to Entra
  2. F signin_flow.py:123 callback(): checks state; H identity/entra_login.py:166 redeem() posts the code + verifier + client secret to Entra's token endpoint
  3. H entra_login.py:184 signed_in(): access token through verify_entra (H identity/entra.py:104: RS256, issuer, audience, expiry, uti); id token's nonce must match; both tokens name the same oid
  4. H identity/__init__.py holder_of(): reads extn.customer_id; Entra writes it as a one-item list ["PH-1001"] (F-114)
  5. F signin_flow.py:84 landing(): policyholder → /; handler (desk.handler role) → /ops/desk; anyone else → 403 "not linked to a policy"
  6. H state/postgres.py:177 PostgresSessionStore.put(): the refresh token, encrypted, into agent_state.sessions; the browser never holds it

The Python objects

# H identity/__init__.py:188 — who the token says this is
Principal(subject="…", customer_id="PH-1001", scopes=frozenset({"claims:read","claims:write"}),
          session="<uti>", party="<azp>", token="eyJ…")

# H contracts/ids.py:90 — what is kept server-side
StoredSession(subject="…", refresh_token="…", updated_at=1791900000)

Sample: The three hops

GET /signin  →  303 Location: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/oauth2/v2.0/authorize
      ?client_id=<ENTRA_APP_ID>&response_type=code&scope=openid profile offline_access
       api://claims-fnol/claims:read api://claims-fnol/claims:write
      &state=…&nonce=…&code_challenge=…&code_challenge_method=S256
   Set-Cookie: signin_flow=gAAAAA…; Path=/signin; HttpOnly; Secure; Max-Age=600

GET /signin/callback?code=0.AX…&state=…
   →  303 Location: /#token=eyJ0eXAi…          (access token in the fragment: no server logs it)
   Set-Cookie: signin_session=gAAAAA…; Max-Age=43200

The access token's claims (v2):
   {"aud": "<ENTRA_APP_ID>", "scp": "claims:read claims:write",
    "extn.customer_id": ["PH-1001"], "oid": "…", "uti": "…", "ver": "2.0"}

Azure: Entra ID (authorize, token, JWKS keys) · Key Vault (client secret, session key) · PostgreSQL (agent_state.sessions)

The policyholder presses send. The page gives the message a delivery id (kept if it has to resend) and posts it with the token. On the server, the harness's /chat handler checks the size, the JSON, the token and the conversation, and only then hands over to the agent.

  3. H serve/__init__.py:147 decode(): body ≤ 8 KiB (413), JSON object (400), non-empty text (400), bearer → verify → as_customer() (401 / 403); a customer_id in the body is ignored
  4. H serve/__init__.py:234 _conversation_for(): store.latest(conversation_id); someone else's conversation → 404
  5. H serve/__init__.py:252 _run_turn(): calls the agent; maps the result to a status code

Part 5 · PythonFirstFunctionReceiveRequestTillRouter From the first function to the router

The agent's turn starts. First the kill switch (is the agent switched on?), then the duplicate check (have we already answered this delivery id?), then the trace span opens, then two gates: is a person holding this conversation, or is a payout waiting? Only if neither applies does the router run.

The journey steps it covers

StepWhat happens (from the 78)On Azure todayHow
14Duplicate check: a repeat gets the earlier answer.runs todayagent_state.requests, scope delivery
15Shared record in the human desk (Chatwoot).not builtPhase 2

The code, in the order it runs

  1. F claims_fnol_app/usage.py:94 Logged.handle: a console line per turn
  2. H entrypoint/switch.py:94 Switched.handle: reads agent.enabled from App Configuration (cached 30 s); false → the paused reply, no route
  3. F claims_fnol/entrypoint/__init__.py:141 Agent.handle: H entrypoint/persist.py:58 delivered() derives the run id from the delivery id (A5)
  4. H requests/__init__.py:156 once(): claims {customer}:{delivery} in agent_state.requests; already answered → AlreadyAnswered; still running → StillRunning (409)
  5. F entrypoint/__init__.py:178 _turn(): span agent.turn (run id, session, user, fingerprint, agent.enabled)
  6. F entrypoint/__init__.py:234 _gates(): a person holds it (H entrypoint/handoff.py:113) or a payout is pending (F entrypoint/pending.py:116 resume) → answer and stop
  7. F entrypoint/__init__.py:204: router.route(text, rules=self.rules)

Part 6 · Router The router decides, from the words alone

Rules, not a model, decide what kind of message this is, in a fixed order: does it need a person? should it be refused? which intent is it? A read-only ask naming exactly one claim or policy is answered by a template (the fixed flow). Everything else goes to the AI loop.

18Small model when unsure.not builtPhase 2
19Several asks split into parts.not builtbasic only: all intents go to the loop together
20Route chosen.runs todayfixed flow, AI loop, a person, or a refusal (no policy search yet)
21–23Fixed flow: look up, fill the template, go to the reply checks.runs todayF entrypoint/direct.py

Part 8 · InsideLoopBeforeModelCall Inside the loop, up to the model's answer

Each step: check the limits, assemble what the model will read (instructions, history, tool results fenced as data), run the injection check, then call the model. The call goes to APIM, never straight to Groq. APIM checks the model is allowed, rate-limits, asks Content Safety about the prompt, forwards to Groq with the key from Key Vault, and screens the answer on the way back.

36Allowed models.runs todayopenai/gpt-oss-120b only
37Token limit.different todayrequest rate (30/min): token limits need a higher APIM tier
38Edge screen with Content Safety.runs todayprompt shield + harm categories, F0 free tier
39Pick a healthy backend.not builtone backend (Groq)

43Gateway counts tokens.runs todayllm-emit-token-metric → App Insights

Part 9 · InsideLoopAfterModelCallToolCallToolResponse After the model: tool calls and their results

The model either answers in words or asks for tools. If it asks for a tool, each call gets an idempotency key, is checked (is it allowed? did the policyholder ask for it?), and goes over MCP to the claims system with an on-behalf-of token. The claims system checks the token itself, does the work in PostgreSQL, and answers. The result goes back to the model as data, and the loop takes another step.

The journey steps it covers

48Needs a person? (a payout)runs todaypart 11
49Gateway for tools.not builtthe agent calls the claims system directly, inside the environment
50Call the tool with a key so a retry cannot act twice.runs todayrun:step:iteration; ledger in agent_state.requests
51Check the result: size cap, hidden instructions, marked as data.runs todayno_instructions_in_result at post_tool
53Save progress.runs todaythe ledger row; the checkpoint at the end of the turn
54–56Limits, no progress, repeat.runs todayoscillation after 3 identical calls

Part 10 · WaitingForAPerson Waiting for a person (DBOS)

A payout above ₹25,000 cannot be paid by the agent. The request_payout tool starts a durable DBOS workflow that waits for a claims handler; the turn ends with "sent to a claims handler" (HTTP 202). When the handler approves on the desk, the workflow pays it under its own login. The same machinery holds a conversation handed to a person.

The journey steps it covers

65Waits as saved records with timers.runs todayDBOS on PostgreSQL
66The decision resumes the work exactly once.runs todaythe approval's digest is checked again by the claims system

  4. H loop/ends.py:104 handed_on(): → NeedsApproval; F entrypoint/pending.py:116 reports on it next turn

Part 11 · AfterLoopResponsePart After the loop: the reply is checked, saved and sent

When the loop ends, the agent adds the claim reference if the reply forgot it, checks whether the conversation now needs a person, updates the facts, checks any promise is backed, and runs the reply rules (no promise of cover, no personal data echoed, money in rupees). Then it saves the conversation and the delivery's answer, and the browser shows the reply.

59Safe fallback.runs todaySAFE_REPLY

61–62Deliver to any window; shown.different todayreturned in the HTTP response

"What's the status of claim CLM-019002?" The message names the claim, so the router sends it down the fixed flow: one read over MCP, one approved sentence — no model, 104 ms, no cost.

A real turn: Rohan Iyer (PH-1001), signed in with Entra, on the Azure deployment, 13 October 2026, in a fresh conversation. Part 12 · Finding this turn again

// the conversation id is in the SessionId column (not in Properties)

What this flow shows

  • Deterministic first pays. The same intent costs 104 ms and nothing here, or 7 s and two model calls in 1b, depending only on whether the message names the claim. A "Check claim CLM-…" button on each claim in the opening would send every such ask down this path.
  • A small inefficiency. The turn calls tools/list twice (about 25 ms each): the direct route lists tools, then the gated client lists them again.
  • The words are not in the trace. agent.captured = False: App Insights has routes, timings, tokens and verdicts, not what Rohan typed. The words above come from the checkpoint and the ledger.
Part 3 · Design · Section 8 · High level design

Flow 1b · Claim status, not naming it

Flow 1b · Claim status, not naming it

"what is the status of my claim" No claim reference, so the router will not guess: the AI loop runs, the model asks for list_claims, then answers with a table — two model calls, 7 seconds.

A real turn: Rohan Iyer (PH-1001), signed in with Entra, on the Azure deployment, 13 October 2026, in a fresh conversation. Every number is from the spans the turn sent to Application Insights and the rows it left in Azure PostgreSQL. The parts are the twelve of The flow in parts. The same question without the reference is Flow 1a; the tables themselves are on Database models.

Part 12 · Finding this turn again

// the conversation id is in the SessionId column (not in Properties)
let ops = AppDependencies | where Name == "agent.turn" and SessionId == "cnv_007191dd0717d964" | distinct OperationId;
union AppDependencies, AppRequests
| where OperationId in (ops)
| order by TimeGenerated asc
| project TimeGenerated, Type, Name, DurationMs, Properties

What this flow shows

  • The router does not guess. "my claim" with nine claims is genuinely ambiguous; the loop answers by listing, which is what the prompt asks for. A single open claim would still go to the loop, because the router counts references in the words, not claims in the database.
  • Most of the wait is not the model. Groq answered in 0.6 s and 1.0 s. The rest is APIM's cold start and token fetch, and Content Safety.
  • Nothing of the loop is in PostgreSQL. The two model calls, the tool request and the full list_claims result live in memory during the turn and as spans in App Insights; only Rohan's words and the final reply are saved, in the checkpoint.
  • The words are not in the trace. agent.captured = False: App Insights has routes, timings, tokens and verdicts, not what Rohan typed. The words above come from the checkpoint and the ledger.
Part 3 · Design · Section 8 · High level design

Flow 2 · Reporting a claim, across two turns

Flow 2 · Reporting a claim, across two turns

"A bus hit my car…", then "pol 1". The first turn cannot register anything — it does not know which policy — so it lists them and asks. The second turn carries the first in its history: the context, and the consent to write.

Both turns are real: Rohan Iyer (PH-1001) on the Azure deployment, 13 October 2026, 14:01, on one open page — the first claim ever reported on this deployment. Spans from Application Insights; rows from Azure PostgreSQL. The parts are those of The flow in parts; tables and classes are explained on Flow 1a.

How turn 2 knew what turn 1 was about

Nothing on the server is "the policy Rohan chose". Turn 2 works because three things travel with the conversation:

  1. The conversation id, kept by the page from turn 1's reply and sent back with "pol 1".
  2. The history, loaded by that id. What the model read in turn 2, step 0:
[system]    You are the claims assistant of a motor insurer, … Register a new claim only on an active
            policy the policyholder holds, and give them its reference and that an assessor will look at it next. …
[user]      A bus hit my car at a signal on MG Road today, rear bumper damaged, nobody hurt.
[assistant] Here are the motor policies you currently have:  | Policy Ref | Product        | Status | Vehicle Reg   | Excess | |------------|----------------|--------|---------------…
[user]      pol 1
                                                 ← 1222 characters, 3 exchanges

The model read its own table — POL-010001 first — next to "pol 1", and called register_claim(id="POL-010001", incident_type="collision"), taking "collision" from the first message. Tool calls and the raw list_policies rows were not in the history: only the words were saved.

  1. The consent. consent.consented() (F entrypoint/consent.py) reads every message the policyholder sent in this conversation. "A bus hit my car" matches the report_claim intent, which allows register_claim; no policy was named, so on any of his policies: register_claim:*. "pol 1" alone allows nothing. The pre_tool check policyholder_asked then let the write through.

Why the resume fix (F-117) matters here. Until 14 October, a reload between the two turns started a new conversation: "pol 1" would have arrived with no history, no table to resolve it against, and no consent to write. Now /opening continues the newest conversation written in the last 24 hours, so the same "pol 1" after a reload works.

The claims system, in one transaction

The holder comes from the token (Verified), never from _meta. Then S store.py _write(): replay check, lock, new claim, remember — all or nothing.

SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2s'
SELECT answer FROM answered WHERE policyholder_id = 'PH-1001' AND key = 'run_fef1576b5602c05a:0:1'          → none
SELECT … FROM policy WHERE id = 'POL-010001' AND policyholder_id = 'PH-1001' FOR UPDATE    → active
SELECT … FROM claim WHERE policy_id = 'POL-010001' AND incident_type = 'collision' AND <open>  → none
INSERT INTO claim … VALUES ('CLM-'||lpad(nextval('claim_number')::text,6,'0'), …, 'registered', …)  → CLM-019002
INSERT INTO answered (policyholder_id, key, operation, answer) VALUES ('PH-1001', 'run_fef1576b5602c05a:0:1', 'register_claim', …)
COMMIT

Two rows, one per turn, each holding the whole conversation so far; the next turn reads only the newest. Turn 1's facts list the two clauses as concerns; turn 2's record what landed: done: register_claim:POL-010001.

What this flow shows

  • A follow-up is only as good as the history. The context and the consent to write both came from turn 1's saved words. That is why losing the conversation on a reload was a real bug, now fixed (F-117).
  • The model resolved "pol 1" from its own words. It worked because the table listed POL-010001 first. A reply that numbered or ordered the policies differently could make "pol 1" ambiguous; a button per policy ("Use POL-010001") would make it certain and skip a model call.
  • The facts name the policy, not the new claim. done: register_claim:POL-010001 — the created CLM-019002 is in the reply and in the ledger's result, but not in facts.records. A hand-off to a person after this turn would carry "a claim was registered on POL-010001" without its reference. Worth a finding.
  • Two guards against a double claim. The agent's ledger row and the claims system's answered row, under the same key — each side protects itself.
  • The router runs per clause. Turn 1 shows three agent.route spans: the message, then each of its two clauses, to know which concerns the reply still owes. Cheap (0 ms each), but it makes traces look as if the router ran three times.
Part 3 · Design · Section 8 · High level design

Flow 3 · Coming back after a reload

Flow 3 · Coming back after a reload

Close the tab, open it again, and carry on. The page asks the server for the policyholder's newest conversation; if it is recent, the earlier messages come back and the next message continues it.

Real runs on the Azure deployment, 14 October 2026, sent by scripts/as_policyholder.py as Rohan Iyer (PH-1001) and, at the desk, Asha Rao (claims handler) — the same HTTP calls the chat page and the desk page make. Spans from Application Insights, rows from Azure PostgreSQL.

The steps

#What the page doesResult
1opens: GET /openingconversation_id: null, nothing earlier — a fresh start
2"A bus hit my car today at a signal, rear bumper damaged, nobody hurt."a new conversation cnv_964aee272863061a; the agent lists the two active policies and asks which
3reload: GET /opening againthe same cnv_964aee272863061a and both earlier messages, 544 ms
4"pol 1" — sent in the conversation /opening returneda claim on POL-010001: context and consent survived the reload
5"new conversation": GET /opening?new=1conversation_id: null

How the reload found the conversation

GET /opening  (Rohan's token: extn.customer_id = ["PH-1001"])
  ConversationFinder.newest_for("PH-1001")
    SELECT state, extract(epoch FROM updated_at)::bigint FROM agent_state.checkpoints
    WHERE customer_id = 'PH-1001' ORDER BY updated_at DESC LIMIT 1
  resume.resumable(found, now, within_hours = App Configuration conversation.resume_hours = 24)
    written 1 minute ago, belongs to PH-1001 → continue it
→ {"reply": "Hello. …", "conversation_id": "cnv_964aee272863061a",
   "earlier": [{"role": "user", "content": "A bus hit my car today …"},
               {"role": "assistant", "content": "I'm sorry—I can't start a claim without knowing which …"}]}

What it shows

  • The fix works live (F-117): a reload continues the conversation, and "pol 1" still has the history it needs — the policy list it refers to and the consent to write that came from the first message.
  • A new finding (F-120). "Your new claim … CLM-019002" — but CLM-019002 is yesterday's claim. The claims system treats "same policy, same incident type, still open" as the same claim and returns it, in the same shape as a new one, so the model calls it new. The answered table shows a second register_claim answer naming CLM-019002; the claim table still has one row.

Flows 4 · 5 · 12 · 14 · Short answers and refusals

Four messages that never reach the model. A policy status and someone else's claim answered by templates, a cover question refused by the router, and an injection attempt stopped before any token is spent.

Real runs on the Azure deployment, 14 October 2026, sent by scripts/as_policyholder.py as Rohan Iyer (PH-1001) and, at the desk, Asha Rao (claims handler) — the same HTTP calls the chat page and the desk page make. Spans from Application Insights, rows from Azure PostgreSQL.

HTTP 200 · 250 ms · refused
I am not able to confirm that. Let me pass you to a colleague who can help.

Routed to the loop, then stopped by no_known_injection at pre_model — before the model was called, so no tokens were spent and APIM was never reached.

What they show

  • Most answers need no model. Three of the four ended before the AI loop, in under 650 ms.
  • Ownership is the far end's job. Flow 14's protection is in the claims system, from the token — not in anything the agent decided.
  • A new finding (F-122). Flow 12's safe reply says "Let me pass you to a colleague who can help" — and no hand-off was created (agent_state.escalations stayed empty). The harness's own fallback makes the kind of unbacked promise its promise gate exists to stop.
Part 3 · Design · Section 8 · High level design

Flows 16 · 17 · Pausing the agent, and the same message twice

Flows 16 · 17 · Pausing the agent, and the same message twice

Two operational guarantees, tested live. A switch in App Configuration pauses every new turn within 30 seconds; a message delivered twice is answered once.

Real runs on the Azure deployment, 14 October 2026, sent by scripts/as_policyholder.py as Rohan Iyer (PH-1001) and, at the desk, Asha Rao (claims handler) — the same HTTP calls the chat page and the desk page make. Spans from Application Insights, rows from Azure PostgreSQL.

az appconfig kv set --key agent.enabled --label dev --value false     13:45:24
  … the agent re-reads App Configuration within 30 s (Cached, H config/settings.py) …
POST /chat "What's the status of claim CLM-010007?"                     (40 s later)
az appconfig kv set --key agent.enabled --label dev --value true      13:46:06
